          v47 change — new screen. Becoming a tutor is a one-time job; keeping your profile current is not. This is a saved-record editor, not the 10-step wizard: sections in any order, each with its own Save, everything pre-filled. Changing your rate no longer means walking past your diploma.

          Two honest notes. The wizard’s step 10 preview could not be reused — it lives inside a sandboxed iframe with its own CSS and clones an availability grid that only exists there — so the preview at the bottom is rebuilt here to match the card students actually see in search. And the wizard never saved its answers anywhere (it gathers all 26 fields, then discards them), so this record is seeded rather than carried over. Wiring the application’s output into this record is a backend task.

          👤

          Edit any section at any time. Certification, education, video and rate are re-reviewed before they change what students see — your current details stay live while a change is checked. Everything else goes live the moment you save.

          Editing re-opens the application form, which is correct while it is still an application. Once you are approved, that form is replaced by the Profile editor and cannot reset your status.

          v47 change — second working admin screen. Required by the re-approval decision: if a tutor’s certification, education, video or rate is re-reviewed, someone has to review it. Old and new values sit side by side. Approving writes the new values into the live profile; rejecting sends the tutor a reason and leaves their current details untouched.

          Pending profile changes

          Only the four reviewed field groups appear here. Name, photo, headline, introduction, experience and languages go live on save and never reach this queue.

          Not built here

          New tutor applications — the queue that approves someone in the first place — is still unbuilt. It needs the application’s own data to exist first, which it does not: the wizard gathers all 26 fields and persists none of them. That wiring is a backend task, not a screen.

          v46 change — new screen. Everything you have bought, everything you are owed, and every credit on your balance, in one place. Before v46 the wireframe could take money but had nowhere to manage it: no cancel, no credit, no receipts you could return to. Order history was moved here from the account overlay rather than copied, so there is still only one order list — the overlay’s Billing item now opens this screen.

          Receipts open as a printable page. The real build serves a PDF here.

          Refund requests

          Refunds go back to the card you paid with. Cancelled 1-on-1 lessons are different — those return a lesson credit, not money. Courses inside 30 days and clear-cut subscription cancellations are approved automatically; cohorts and degree programs are reviewed by a person.

          v46 change — new screen. Rescheduling is self-serve: you pick from the slots your tutor has actually published, up to twice per booking, and only while you are outside the 12-hour window. Nothing is charged. If your tutor has published no slots, the screen offers the cancel-for-full-credit route instead of dead-ending — try Aisha Rahman’s booking to see that branch.

          v46 change — new screen. v45 had “Receipt” links in the billing panel that went nowhere. They now open this. It is a printable page, not a PDF — a wireframe that opens offline cannot generate one, and the real build would serve a PDF at this URL.

          v46 change — the first real admin screen. The console was a placeholder listing six things it would one day need. This builds the one that generates support tickets on day one. Cohort and degree refunds are the cases a student cannot self-serve, so they land here. The buttons work: approve, approve a partial amount, deny with a reason the student sees, or leave an internal note.

          Refund requests

          Auto-approved cases still appear here for the audit trail, marked as such. A denial cannot be saved without a reason — the student is shown it.

          What this queue does not do yet

          Issuing goodwill credit directly to a student, bulk-refunding a cancelled cohort, and reversing a payout that has already released. The third one is deliberate — the agreed model is that TrioEdX absorbs a refund approved after payout rather than clawing back from a tutor.

          Placeholder — not built

          Admin console

          An admin console needs its own requirement pass before it can be drawn. On the evidence of this wireframe it would have to cover at least: user management (the accounts below), tutor approvals (the pending-review queue the tutor flow already creates), course moderation, payouts and refunds, coupons, and platform settings including the revenue-share tiers.

          Several of those already exist as tutor- or student-facing screens, so the question is which of them an admin oversees rather than owns — which is exactly the decision a requirement pass has to make.
